Kubjikātantra, First Chapter.
Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Lord, Ancient One!
O Nandīśa, among all beings, you are the stainless one, higher than the highest.
"O Lord, what is being recited by you, and for what purpose?
O Lord of Gods, by what means may one attain the stainless state? (1.2)
If you have compassion for me, speak that which is the most essential of the essential;
reveal the rules for the conduct of the observance and the means of accomplishment.
Furthermore, I wish to hear all that which is called the Śabdabrahman—the consciousness of all beings—for the benefit of spiritual practitioners. (1.4)
If he were my lord of life, reveal the hidden meaning;
O Mahādeva, swear an oath to me and reveal the vast womb.

Furthermore, reveal to me that essence which is the nature of the accomplishment of latent impressions (vāsanā), as well as the accomplishment of existence (bhāva), and that which is attainable through the core of the Vedas.
Sadāśiva said:
"Excellent, excellent! O Goddess, listen to that which has been spoken by you from me—the essence of essences, O Goddess, higher than the high, and supreme among the supreme."
Higher than eternal bliss, infinite, and having the nature of the Śabdabrahman—truth, truth, again truth; truth, truth, again and again. (1/8)
It must not be revealed, it must not be revealed, it must never be revealed;
this is the supreme secret, difficult to find in the three worlds. (1/9)
O Great Goddess, having known which you have become a lord of yogis, Sadāśiva;
it cannot be described even in a thousand future births. (1/10)
"O Goddess, out of affection for you, I shall tell it; listen to that.
It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret by you once again. (1.11)
O Great Goddess, this must never be revealed in the presence of a bound soul (paśu)—that is, one who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, or the Yonimudrā. 1.12
O lady of excellent limbs, it is not accomplished even by hundreds of millions of kalpas;
O Sovereign of the Sages, I shall now declare the great mantra and the true meaning of the mantra.

O beloved of the vital breath, by means of that mere consciousness one becomes a lord of all accomplishments; it is through the purity of intention alone that the purpose of the mantra is attained. (1.14)
Merely by means of knowledge alone, a man is certainly liberated while living;
[she is] Kālī, Tārā, Mahādevī, Bhuvaneśī, and Ṣoḍaśī. (1.15)
O Dear One, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Vidyā, Dhūmāvatī, Vagalā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā are proclaimed [as the goddesses]. (1.16)
Worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as by the four Vedas; the Goddess who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, she is hidden within millions of cosmic eggs. 1/17
The Goddess is the bestower of the fourfold aims of life and the giver of the state of Nirvāṇa;
she consists of the vital breath of the God of gods and embodies the nature of all the gods. 1.18
Accessible through meditation by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, she is the goddess who pervades the universe;
she is the Great Goddess in the form of Viṣṇu, the cause of creation and sustenance. (1.19)
Situated in the Jewel Pavilion, she is the destroyer of Mahākāla;
by the mere hearing of her [name], the practitioner becomes liberated while living. (1.20)
Those who have not been born into [any] lineage and are intent on accomplishing Kālī—hearing that, all their ancestors dance with delighted minds. (1.21)
All the kinnaras dance and the practitioners sing verses:
"Even though this great vidyā is not to be given away, in the Kali age it bestows its full fruit. (1.22)
In the three preceding ages, worship should be performed according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti;
however, in the Kali age, the wise man should sacrifice to the gods according to the injunctions declared in the Āgamas.
For the gods do not become propitious in the Kali age through other methods;
O Goddess Kālikā, you are the bestower of liberation and the one who grants swift results in the Kali age. (1.24)
One should receive the great lore that destroys sin from the mouth of the Guru;
Brahmāṇī performs the creation, but Brahmā never does. (1.25)
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, Brahmā is a ghost (preta), of this there is no doubt;
O Goddess, Vaiṣṇavī indeed performs the protection, but Viṣṇu never does.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, Viṣṇu is undoubtedly a ghost (preta);
Rudrāṇī performs the act of devouring, but Rudra never does.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, Rudra is undoubtedly a *preta*;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others are likewise proclaimed to be insentient. (1.28)

O Goddess, without primordial nature (prakṛti), the best of practitioners would certainly be incapable of performing any action, since it is through her that he performs dharma, adharma, and so forth. (1.29)
It bestows grace upon all that, O Vāmikā, there is no doubt;
and it must be performed according to the traditional injunctions, O Maheśvarī. 1/30.
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who are devoid of the traditional lineage (sampradāya), there shall be no fruit;
that which is Kṛṣṇā is indeed Kṛṣṇa, and likewise is proclaimed to be Brahmā.
He who contemplates non-difference has liberation held in the palm of his hand;
he who contemplates difference is a fool and a sinner. (1.32)
One who creates division shall go to hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
but he who contemplates non-differentiation is a yogi—of this there is no doubt. (1.33)
In the Kali age, having assumed a dark form and sporting in Vṛndāvana,
she deludes the entire world with the playful sound of her flute.
Kālikā is the destroyer of suffering and Durgā is the vanquisher of difficulties;
even though she is white, in the Kali age she assumes a black state, appearing in a blue form.
Because she bestows speech through her divine play, she is Nīlasarasvatī;
because she always delivers [beings] from saṃsāra, she is celebrated as Tārā and Tāriṇī. (1.36)
She is celebrated as Bhuvaneśī because she is the protector of the worlds;
the Goddess is also called Bhuvaneśī because she effects both creation and sustenance. (1.37)
When the goddess Śrīdyutrī is proclaimed as Śrīvidyā, she is the Great Goddess Nirguṇā, celebrated as Ṣoḍaśī. (1.38)
Bhairavī is the destroyer of suffering and the annihilator of the misery of Yama;
she is celebrated as Bhairavī, the consort of Kālabhairava. (1.39)
The goddess Triśakti is the granter of desires, as is Chinnā, the sovereign of the gods;
the great goddess Triguṇā is the deluder, yet she is certainly the giver of liberation.
Dhūmāvatī is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the destroyer of the Asura Dhūmra;
she is the Great Goddess in the form of smoke, the bestower of the fourfold aims of life. 1.41
She is the mother of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the benefactress of all beings;
she is known as the goddess Vāruṇī in the syllable *va* and as the bestower of perfection in the syllable *ga*.
In the syllable *lā*, the Earth is proclaimed as the essence of consciousness;
she is Mātaṅgī, who, by her intoxicated nature, is the destroyer of the demon Mataṅga. (1.43)
The goddess Mātaṅgī is proclaimed as the one who carries away all transgressions;
the goddess Kamalā is likewise celebrated as the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha. (1.44)
The goddess dwelling in Pātāla, beautiful and in the form of Lakṣmī—these are the ten Mahāvidyās, and they are called the Siddhavidyā. || 1/45 ||
She eternally bestows dharma, artha, and liberation, granting the fruits of the four aims of life; by whatever means possible, she grants the full fruit in the Kali age. (1.46)
It is especially liberating from sin for those who are destitute and miserable, as well as for heretics, the deceitful, the meritless, and the revilers. (1.47)
"O beautiful one, O auspicious lady, this must never be disclosed by me to sons who are not devoted, nor to those who lack obedience; this is my firm vow. (1.48)
O Maheśvarī, one should indeed give [this] to one endowed with all the auspicious marks;
there is certainly nothing equal to these among the three worlds, it is certain. (1/49)
By reciting it even once, one is liberated from all sins;
O Goddess of gods, by mere remembrance, one is released from the bondage of worldly existence. (1.50)
The eternal Śiva is to be known as both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessed of attributes (saguṇa).
From that which is indeed devoid of attributes, the three drops (vindu) were born. 1/51.
O Maheśvarī, there was the Brahmabindu, the Viṣṇubindu, and the Rudrabindu;
from that Bindu arose Nāda, and from Nāda the emergence of Śakti.
O Maheśānī, she is the form of sound (nāda), the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness; and from that very sound, O Maheśvarī, the half-moon (ardhacandra) is produced. 1/53.
From the three and a half bindus arises the serpent-like Kulakuṇḍalinī, the eternal Goddess whose form is Brahman, both devoid of attributes and possessed of attributes. 1/54
The Goddess, whose form is consciousness, is of the nature of Brahman and eternal;
the Goddess, whose form is consciousness, is the illuminator of all beings. (1.55)
O Great Goddess, she consists of the three qualities and illuminates that which possesses the three qualities;
yet she is to be known as devoid of qualities, the very form of Brahman, and absolute. (1.56)
The Great Goddess possesses six qualities and is the illuminator of the six cakras;
O Maheśānī, she possesses four qualities and is the source of the splendor of the four Vedas. (1.57)
The Vidyā whose essence is the moon and sun illuminates the moon and sun;
she is the Great Goddess possessing all qualities, who brings forth the light of the entire universe. (1.58)
O Great Goddess, you possess eightfold qualities and manifest the eight supernatural powers;
O beautiful lady of the gods, you are the mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (1.59)
The Goddess, whose nature is the locus of mantra, is eternally composed of all mantras;
she is the Great Goddess of singular quality, whose very form is the single syllable. (1.60)
The Great Goddess who is twofold is the progenitor of the two-syllabled mantra;
the Great Goddess who is threefold is proclaimed as the three-syllabled mantra. (1.61)
That Goddess possesses four qualities and gives birth to four syllables;
O Maheśānī, she possesses nine qualities and reveals the nine syllables. (1.62)
In the tenth and eleventh [months], she has the form of ten and eleven;
and in the twelfth and thirteenth, she is the twelfth [digit] consisting of the thirteen gods.
She consists of fourteen aspects and illuminates fourteen;
the Goddess consists of fifteen aspects and illuminates fifteen. (1.64)
O Supreme Goddess, the sixteenth [vow] arises from the sixteen;
endowed with seventeen groups, it is proclaimed as the seventeenth. (1.65)
The eighteen Great Vidyās consist of eighteen qualities;
endowed with twenty-eight qualities, she is the supreme form worthy of worship. (1.66)
A great vidyā consists of twenty syllables and has the nature of supreme bliss;
mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as mālā-mantras. (1.67)
Endowed with twenty-one qualities, possessed of twenty-two, and proclaimed as having twenty-three, twenty-four, and twenty-five [qualities]. (1.68)
Endowed with twenty-six qualities and consisting of twenty-six qualities, she is endowed with twenty-eight qualities and is proclaimed as twenty-eightfold. (1.69)
The twenty-ninth is proclaimed as the Great Goddess Mahāvidyā;
those beginning with the thirtieth up to the sixty-fourth are proclaimed as the long mantras. (1.70)
Likewise, O Pārvatī, neuter mantras, those ending solely in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, those joined with *svāhā*, and those that are *śakti*-mantras; 1.71.
"Any one of these mantras is proclaimed as the Puruṣa.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Kubjikātantra, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord.
The Second Chapter.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall explain the supreme essence of the meaning of the mantra, without which recitation, worship, and so forth will never achieve success anywhere. (2.1)
Therefore, with every effort, listen to the mantra of Girijā.
The letter *ka* is said to be the granter of desires, and the letter *ra* is the destroyer of sin.
In the letter *ī*, Śambhu is present, immeasurable and endowed with *nāda* and *bindu*.
The Great Goddess is of the nature of sound, devoid of qualities, and has the form of Brahman.
The letter *ka* bestows dharma and artha and grants all perfections;
the letter *ma* is the form of Brahman, and it is both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*). (2.4)
The syllable *U* is a mass of splendor that destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils;
the syllable *Ī* is the form of Durgā, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of human life.
The single-syllable great vidyā is the embodiment of all vidyās.
The letter *ka* is declared to be Varuṇa, the sustainer of the life-force of the world. (2.6)
The letter *ra* should be known as Śaṅkara, the eternal benefactor of all;
in the letter *ī* is the goddess Tāriṇī, who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence. (2.7)
The syllable *ka* is said to be Keśava, the cause of the state of Nirvāṇa;
the syllable *ra* is this form of fire, the burner of the suffering of worldly existence. (2.8)
In the letter *ī* is the Goddess Mātṛkā, who bestows the four aims of life;
when the Goddess possesses qualities (*saguṇā*), she is the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). (2.9)
The letter *ha*, however, is declared to be Śiva, the eternal embodiment of knowledge;
it is the god who bestows liberation and nirvāṇa, and grants all spiritual accomplishments. (2.10)
The letter *ra* resembles the sun and is the supreme burner of sins;
in the letter *u* resides the goddess Bhairavī, the destroyer of all dangers. (2.11)
O Maheśānī, she who is in the form of sound is proclaimed to be beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).
And in the letter *ha* is Mahāviṣṇu, the destroyer of great sins. (2.12)
The letter *ra* is of the nature of the moon and bestows immortality;
in the letter *u* resides the goddess Mohinī, who causes the delusion of the world. (2.13)
It is the destroyer of great suffering and the eradicator of the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils;
the letter *ha* is Sadāśiva, and indeed, the letter *u* is Brahmā. (2.14)
It is devoid of qualities, consisting of sound and the point (nāda-bindu), and is the absolute state of liberation;
by the mere remembrance of this, one obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices. (2.15)
The letter *ha* is said to be Śambhu, adorned with the letter *ra*, while the letter *ī* is the Supreme Goddess, who is eternally composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*). (2.16)
The letter *da* is all the gods and the warder-off of all difficulties;
the letter *kṣa* is Viṣṇu, the giver of sacred fields and the destroyer of great sins. (2.17)
In the syllable *ha*, all the deities reside, who again bestow all desired objects;
and in the syllable *la* is the goddess Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas. (2.18)
In the letter *e* is the form of the womb (*yoni*), the supreme seed of the universe;
in the letter *ka*, the earth is said to be present, along with its mountains, forests, and groves. (2.19)
In the syllable *ka*, O Goddess, resides Sakalā, the bestower of all accomplishments;
in the syllable *la*, there is the Earth Goddess, who grants the fruit of the gift of the earth. (2.20)
In the syllable *ī*, O Goddess, she is Sakalā, the creator of the lords of all;
in the syllable *ka*, she is Sundarī; and in the syllable *e*, she is Yonirūpiṇī.
O Goddess, you are the bestower of dharma, artha, and kāma; the destroyer of wicked daityas;
the supreme, the most excellent, and furthermore, a portion of the Supreme Self.
In the syllable *ka* is Mahābrahmā; the syllable *ka* has the form of Viṣṇu;
in the syllable *ka* is Mahādeva, and the letter *ra* is indeed Brahmāṇī. (2.23)
Vaiṣṇavī is the letter with the medial *repha* (ṛ); Rudrāṇī is the *repha* followed by [another] *repha*.
The beloved letter *ī* grants desires when adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*. (2.24)
The letter *ha* is indeed desire; that letter *ha* has the form of the sun.
The letter *u* is the goddess Ṣoḍaśī, and the letter *ū* is Bhuvaneśvarī. (2.25)
The great mantras are proclaimed to be joined with the *nāda* and the *bindu*;
the letter *ha* is yogic sleep, and the letter *ha* is the supreme, all-pervading Lord. (2.26)
The letter *ī* is Kāmadā, *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), and the letter *ra* is considered Paraśiva.
And that letter *ra*, O Great Goddess, is adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*. (2.27)
And Svāhā herself, O Maheśānī, is proclaimed as a mass of splendor;
she is the single-syllabled Great Vidyā, the eternal Brahma-vidyā. (2.28)
The three-syllabled great vidyā is proclaimed as having three qualities;
the eight-syllabled great vidyā directly bestows the fruit of liberation. (2.29)
The twenty-fold Mahāvidyā is proclaimed as the Eight Siddhis;
the twenty-first Mahāvidyā is Maheśvarī, whose beginning is the Praṇava. (2.30)
O Sovereign of the Gods, this mantra of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others is proclaimed to consist of the syllables A, U, and M. (2.31)
The single-syllable great mantra is the very nature of consciousness and bliss;
the Vidyā enclosed within the Praṇava is designated as the "Bridge" (Setu). (2.32)
The great mantra of Siddhakālī is remembered as the bestower of the fulfillment of desires;
the letter *Ha* is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), and the letter *Ra* is the giver of liberation (*nirvāṇa*). (2.33)
The letter *u* is the consort of Śambhu, whose nature is the power (*śakti*) of Śiva; the seed-syllable of Kāma is likewise encased by desire (*kāma*) and illusion (*māyā*). (2.34)
Then the mantra of Kāmeśvara bestows the fruit of all desires;
within the nine-syllable [mantra], the seed-syllable of desire is the supreme Śambhu, whose form is consciousness. (2.35)
In the nine-syllable [mantra], the *kūrca* seed-syllable is the eternal form of Brahman;
in the nine-syllable [mantra], "Dakṣiṇā" bestows the supreme reality of Kālikā. (2.36)
In the fourteenth [syllable], the seed-syllable of Kāma is proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavī;
in the eleventh, the seed-syllable of Kāma becomes the savior from saṃsāra. (2.37)
The word "namaḥ" bestows enjoyment and grants the fruit of royal enjoyment;
the fifteen-syllable great mantra grants the fruit of all desires. (2.38)
The seed-syllable of Māyā and the seed-syllable of Krodha are each the very form of Śiva;
Guhyakālī consists of sixteen syllables and is the absolute embodiment of Brahman.
The Goddess who effects creation and maintenance, consisting of the world and possessing a hundred divisions,
is the nine-syllable Great Vidyā situated above the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma).

The secret one is the bestower of liberation in the world, the granter of the four aims of life; she is the Goddess of Speech, all the deities, and the supreme one in the form of the syllable *ai*. (2.41)
The letter *ī* is the consort of Śambhu; the syllable *phaṭ* is the embodiment of the Cakra;
she is Kāmākhyā, Bhuvaneśī, the Absolute, and the one whose form is desire. (2.42)
The great goddess Bhadrakālī, the sovereign of the world and the mistress of serpents, always supports the earth in the form of a great serpent-queen. (2.43)
The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma) is Maheśa, the eternal one of eight forms;
the seed-syllable Kūrca is Mahāviṣṇu, and the syllable Phaṭ is the destroyer of sins.
In the mantra of Śmaśānakālikā, the five-syllable [mantra] is proclaimed;
it consists of the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), the Lord of the Arts (HRĪM), and that which alone assumes the form of desire (KLĪM). (2.45)
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Māyā effects concealment by illusion;
O Maheśānī, the Kūrca seed-syllable bestows great merit. (2.46)
The letter *ī* is the Supreme Power (*paramāśakti*), the bestower of liberation upon yogis;
and the letter *kṣa*, O Great Goddess, is proclaimed to be the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). (2.47)
And the letter *A*, O Great Goddess, is proclaimed to be the Earth;
by the mere remembrance of this, the practitioner becomes liberated while living. (2.48)
By merely reciting it once, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
hear now, O auspicious lady, what the fruit is that comes from its mere remembrance. (2.49)
All sins, beginning with the killing of a Brahmin, certainly go to destruction;
it yields the fruit of ten million times ten million great holy places and ten thousand horse sacrifices. (2.50)
The best of practitioners shall not undergo rebirth on earth;
and as for the recitation [of this], O Maheśānī, it is simply impossible to describe. (2.51)
Having recited the mantra encased within the *praṇava* (oṃ), or encased by the *māyā* (hrīṃ) syllable, one hundred and eight times, and [the mantra of] Gajāntaka one thousand times; // 2.52 //
O beautiful goddess, one should recite the mantra for the purpose of pacifying its defects;
O Maheśvarī, the mantra is of two kinds: devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessed of attributes (saguṇa).
By whatever means possible, one shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments;
having encased [the mantra] within the *mātṛkā*, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. (2.54)
O Goddess, one should recite it a thousand times for the pacification of defects in the mantra;
the wise person should recite the Mātṛkā both in direct and reverse order. (2.55)
Success shall consist of the eight groups [of syllables], and one shall obtain the fruit of all desires;
this is proclaimed as the Great Vidyā of the Great Goddess Tārā. (2.56)
The five-syllabled great vidyā reveals the five elements;
the five-syllabled great vidyā is endowed with five rays of light. (2.57)
O Sovereign of the Sun, one should understand the Kālikā and Tāriṇī mantras, their non-duality, and the meaning of the mantra; she who consists of the universe has a hundredfold divisions. (2.58)
Just as Kālī is, so is Tārā; thus have the mantras been proclaimed.
O beautiful goddess, [I shall explain] the sādhana, the yantra, the mantra, and the meaning of the mantra. (2.59)
"Out of affection for you, I shall proclaim this most wonderful secret.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Kubjikātantra.
The third chapter.
The venerable Śiva said: Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the supreme meaning of the mantra.
Bhuvaneśī is the Great Vidyā, saluted by all the Āmnāyas. || 3/1 ||
The letter *ha* is the form of Brahman, illuminating the entire universe;
the letter *ra* is the light of the moon, and the letter *ī* is, moreover, supreme. (3.2)
O fair-faced one, the Vidyā consisting of the Nirguṇa, Nāda, and Bindu, which produces delight in the middle [channel], was cursed by Brahmā when it was being practiced. 3/3.
From the syllable *ai* arises the Goddess Earth, eternal and of universal form;
she is the womb-like form, O Great Goddess, the destroyer of great sins. (3.4)
The letter *ha* is the supreme bindu, and this letter *ra* is the protector;
with the letter *ī*, O Great Goddess, she bestows all desired objects. (3.5)
The Vidyā worshipped by Śiva bestows the supreme reality;
from the letter *Ā*, she is the form of the Sun, Māyā who illumines the universe. (3.6)
From the syllable *krau* arises the creative power (*janikā śakti*), known as Kāmākhyā, the bestower of liberation;
the letter *śa* is the form of Kṛṣṇa, devoted to the welfare of all living beings. (3.7)
In the letter *ī* she is of the nature of stability, and in the letter *r* she is the eternal and primeval one;
she is the power of resonance (*nāda-śakti*) whose form is consciousness, bestowing supreme bliss. (3.8)
O Goddess, the letter *ha* is Vāsudeva, the bestower of the four aims of life, and its form is Lakṣmī; the letter *ra* is the bestower of creation. (3.9)
In the syllable *ī* is the goddess Tripurā, whose nature consists of Nāda, Bindu, and Śiva;
in the syllable *na* is the power Pālikā; and in the syllable *ma* is the destroyer. (3.10)
The syllable *namaḥ* is declared to be the fulfiller of desires and the supreme means for accomplishing all goals;
in the letter *bha* resides the Goddess Bhagavatī, and in the letter *va*, she whose essence is Varuṇa.
In the syllable *ta* is the goddess Tāriṇī, the beloved of the life-breath of the universe;
in the syllable *ī* is the goddess Mātṛkā, remembered as the mother of the worlds. (3.12)
In the syllable *ma*, she is of the nature of Śiva and the bestower of auspiciousness to the universe;
in the syllable *a*, she is of the nature of Rudra and the form of the destruction of the universe. (3.13)
In the syllable *ha* is the goddess Yoginī, who is the embodiment of yoga for yogins;
in the syllable *e* is the goddess Jananī, the Mother from whom the universe is born. (3.14)
In the letter Śa is the power of the universe (viśvaśakti), and in the letter Va is the protectress (paripālinī).
The goddess Ra is the bestower of knowledge (jñānadā) and the illuminator of all knowledge (sarvajñānaprakāśinī). (3.15)
And in the letter *ī*, O Great Goddess, she is the increaser of consciousness and bliss.
Now listen, O Great Goddess: in the letter *r*, he is the beloved of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (3.16)
In the syllable *na*, the goddess Vandinī is the increaser of joy for all;
and Svāhā, the great vidyā, is proclaimed as Agnijihvā. (3.17)
The Great Vidyā beginning with the Praṇava is considered the bestower of knowledge upon the wise;

O Goddess, when it begins with the seed-syllable *śrī*, it bestows prosperity;

The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) situated at the three peaks is the very nature of Mahāyoga;

The Fourth Chapter. Śiva said: O Pārvatī, listen with diligence to the mantra of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā.
It must not be disclosed, O Great Goddess; it must never be disclosed.

by the letter *ka* is the eye of the Goddess, and by the letter *la* is the *tārikā*. (4.2)
In the letter *ī*, the space between the eyebrows; the *nāda* and *bindu* are certainly the *śikhā*.
The *kūrca* seed-syllable, the *kapāla*, the *vāgbhava*, and the very word itself [are located there]. (4.3)
Bhuvaneśī is the nose, and Vajra is proclaimed to be the throat;
Trayonāda is of the nature of Śakti, and Rocanīyaka is the tongue. (4.4)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should know Aghora together with Svāhā;
this five-syllabled great vidyā is proclaimed as Ḍākinī. (4.6)
The eleven-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as Varṇinī;
she is the goddess who bestows wealth, grants liberation, and yields the fruit of all desires. (4.7)
And at the time of his worship, O beautiful one, in all the worlds, there is no other worshiper—neither a husband nor even a king. (4.8)
In the propitiation of the Great Goddess, one will certainly receive a blow from a weapon;
from that blow from a weapon, liberation arises—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Sovereign of the Gods. (4.9)
Listen, O Goddess, ever auspicious one, you who provide protection to your devotees, to Dhūmāvatī, the Great Vidyā, who possesses the power of great yoga. (4.10)
I shall proclaim its mantra; listen, O beloved of Hara!
In the syllable *dhakāra* is Sarvadhamanī, and in the syllable *ukāra*, Pālinī is remembered. (4.11)
The goddess who has the form of Caitanya, the consort of Mahākāla;
the goddess who destroys in Dhṛkāra, the bringer of the great dissolution. (4.12)
In the syllable MA she is Mārarūpā, and in the syllable Ā she is Ratisundarī;
in the syllable VA she is Kāmarūpā, and in the syllable TI she is Tīkṣṇadhāriṇī. (4.13)
O Maheśānī, Svāhā is indeed proclaimed as Bhairavī;
she is also the great vidyā Vagalā. O beloved, hear her mantra.
By the mere knowledge of that, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
O Goddess, the *praṇava* is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), and the nose is indeed the triple power (*triśakti*). (4.16)

and Svāhā is the great vidyā, the form of sacrifice, who consumes the oblation. (4.21)
And Mātaṅgī is the Great Vidyā, established in all tantras.
Listen, O Goddess Mahābhadre, you who provide protection for devotees! 4/22

And Svāhā is indeed of the nature of Brahman, established by Brahmā.

By the mere knowledge of whom one certainly attains prosperity;

Fifth Chapter (p.
7). Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all gods, benefactor of the worlds!"
O Goddess, reveal to me that consciousness which bestows the fourfold aims of life.
Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most wonderful consciousness;
it is a supreme secret, a profound mystery, which must be guarded by you once more. (5.2)

O Goddess, by means of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), that which has resounded through the path, having taken recourse to the state of phonemes (varṇabhāva) through the process of transformation, becomes endowed with qualities (saguṇātmaka) while being essentially devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Likewise, having pierced the six chakras, the eternal form of sound (śabda-rūpa), conjoined with nāda and bindu, is proclaimed as consciousness (caitanya). (5.4)
Alternatively, O lotus-eyed one, listen to another method by which [practices] such as recitation and worship do not succeed. (5.5)
O Goddess, the supreme syllable is strung upon the center of the unstruck sound (anāhata),
having emerged from the region of the throat by way of the path of the Suṣumṇā.
And consciousness, O Great Goddess, takes the form of yoga for yogis;
it appears in the form of letters within the thousand-petalled lotus through the process of transformation. (5.7)
One should then contemplate the Goddess, who resides in the center of the pericarp, endowed with the *nāda* and the *bindu*, and who is the supreme consciousness. (5.8)
O Maheśvarī, the syllables of the mantra are strung upon the power of consciousness;
O Goddess, one should contemplate them when they are situated within the thousand-petaled lotus.
She is consciousness in the form of mantra, bestowing the bliss of consciousness;
she is consciousness as the power of sound (nāda-śakti), and consciousness in the form of phonemes (varṇa). || 5/10 ||
In Maṇipurī, one should always contemplate that which is the life-force of mantras;
or else, O lady of excellent complexion, listen to it in another way. (5.11)

O Sovereign of the Gods, having first uttered the seed-syllable of desire (Kāmabīja), the seed-syllable of Ramā (Ramābīja), and the seed-syllable of Śakti (Śaktibīja), one should thereafter recite the Mātṛkā.
One should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times while it is being folded; one obtains ten million times ten million times that merit—of this there is no doubt. || 5/13 ||
Alternatively, O Pārvatī, hear of consciousness in another way, by the mere knowledge of which one certainly beholds the Supreme. (5.14)
One should contemplate the root mantra situated in the center of the solar disc;
the root-vidyā itself should be recited one hundred and eight times. (5.15)
There, one should contemplate the Guru as the eternal form of Śiva;
and there, one should contemplate Śakti as the eternal form of Brahman.
For one who thus contemplates or recites [this] to the beautiful goddess of the gods, nothing in this world is unattainable; O Goddess, liberation is held in the palm of his hand. (5.17)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Kubjikātantra. || 0 || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter. Now, O Maheśānī, O lady with a face like the autumnal moon, I shall declare that which is exceedingly supreme and secret, never to be disclosed under any circumstances.

This is the supreme secret, most hidden, and honored by all the gods; it is inaccessible even to those learned in the four Vedas, yet it is the means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (6.2)
O Great Goddess, O beautiful lady of the gods, it is worshipped by all the sacred traditions;
it is to be concealed, most to be concealed, and to be concealed, O Sovereign of the Gods. (6.3)
This must not be disclosed, O Goddess Pārvatī, like one's own private parts;
at midnight, with hair disheveled, naked, and accompanied by the Śakti.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon his chosen goddess, who is the embodiment of yoga for yogis;
he should place the ankle of his left foot against the secret region. (6.5)
Having made the body steady, one should place the tongue against the palate;
and the pair of eyes should be fixed on the tip of the nose, O Maheśvarī. (6.6)
Having likewise brought [the breath] to the level of the throat, one should contemplate the auspicious river,
the goddess in the form of a serpent, who dwells in the *mūlādhāra*.
In the morning, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess, who is seated within the orb of fire in the ādhāra-lotus, possessing four arms and nourished by supreme nectar.
The Great Goddess, of dark complexion, seated upon a great lotus throne,
always holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons in her right hands.
The eternal one, holding a sword and a skull-bowl in her left hand, with loosened hair, a smiling face, and dwelling in the cremation ground. (6.10)
She has protruding teeth, her body extends to the south, her hair is disheveled, and she is naked;
she wears a girdle made from a multitude of corpses and has a smiling face. (6.11)
She is Sadāśivā, wearing a dangling garland of severed heads, with her right foot placed upon the heart of a corpse. (6.12)
For the sake of pleasure, Mahākāla approached another woman who was intensely longing for him and possessed the three marks of beauty, like the moon and the sun. (6.13)
The goddess, bearing a crescent moon and possessing full, elevated breasts,
was accompanied on the four sides by auspicious yet fiercely howling [attendants].
Inaccessible even to those who know the four Vedas, adorned by all the gods,
she grants desires, assumes any form at will, and acts as a protector for her devotees.
One should salute the formidable Dakṣiṇakālikā, who bestows the fourfold aims of life;
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate her as the Svādhiṣṭhāna, having the form of the moon.
There, having meditated upon the goddess, who is stainless and possesses universal forms, with her hands granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, O beautiful one among the gods. (6.17)
The Goddess, bearing a bow and arrows, and again holding a noose and a goad, is joined with a Bāṇaliṅga; she is blue in color and possesses the brilliance of fire. (6.18)
The great goddess with a quivering tongue, whose form is Viṣṇu, eternal,
with ears adorned by a pair of locks of hair, the destroyer of wicked asuras.
Clad in a tiger skin, she dwells in the *brahmarandhra*;
her face is serene and pleasant, like a blooming lotus with a smiling countenance.
In Maṇipūra, one should meditate upon the eternal mass of splendor—naked, with a formidable face, loose hair, and four arms. (6.21)
The Great Goddess is red in color, wearing a red skin;
the Great Goddess is seated in the lotus posture and adorned with all the nāgas. (6.22)
She who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; she who is worshipped by the gods;
the Goddess who bestows dharma and wealth, and who provides protection to her devotees. (6.23)
To the Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, who again deludes the worlds, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the Enchantress, the virtuous one who incessantly grants knowledge; 6/24.
She is beautiful, delightful, and charming, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life; she is peaceful, beloved by those who are tranquil, yet fierce, being the destroyer of formidable demons.
To the one who loves honey and meat, Kṛṣṇā, who brings joy to Yaśodā, the Great Goddess accessible through devotion, who dwells in Mahākāla; || 6/26 ||
One should contemplate the eternal Mother of all, worshipped by the gods;
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate the Supreme Deity within the Anāhata [cakra]. (6.27)
O Śivā, [I salute] the great goddess with eight arms, red in color and possessing three powers,
who holds a bow, an arrow, a sword, and a discus.
The goddess who holds a noose and a goad, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā, who bears the crescent moon, and whose breasts are full and elevated. (6.29)
One should thus contemplate the Goddess Mahāmāyā, seated upon a lotus throne, established on a great lotus seat, and proceeding by way of Brahman. (6.30)
And in the pure great wheel, one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess—the ten-armed Great Goddess, yellow in color and eternal. (6.31)
The Goddess, seated upon the Kāma-bīja, holds in her right hands a skull-cup, a shield, a sword, a mirror, and a chowrie.
The Great Goddess, seated upon a great lion throne, holds in her left hands a sword, a great lotus, a flaying knife, a noose, and a goad. || 6.33 ||
Clad in divine garments, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
she was a celestial beauty worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva.
O Maheśānī, the wise one should meditate upon her at the Ājñā-cakra as having two arms, mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, two-armed, and exceedingly beautiful. (6.35)
Holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with various jewels, endowed with a crown of matted hair, and decorated with the crescent moon. || 6/36 ||
Adorned with a jeweled girdle and embellished with a garland of gems,
she is clothed in red garments and served by the Lord of Kamalā.

O Goddess, one should meditate upon her who is the pacifier of the suffering of saṃsāra, who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, and whose form is meditation, by means of the path of the suṣumṇā.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess through the yoga of piercing the six cakras; one should likewise meditate upon the Supreme Goddess in the thousand-petaled lotus. (6.39)
One should place within that [mandala] the wandering god of love (Kāma), adorned with five arrows,
as well as all the sacred fords (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā and nectar upon a leaf.
O Great Goddess, it is adorned with all the seasons beginning with spring;
O Great Goddess, it is white in color and possesses an excellent thousand petals.
O Goddess, it is joined with all the gods, endowed with all powers,
consisting of all mantras, and adorned by the four Vedas.
One should meditate there upon the eleventh Mahādeva, who is the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and upon the goddess seated upon a pericarp of golden hue. (6.43)

O Goddess, [I salute] the Supreme Śiva, who consists of consciousness, who is attainable through meditation, eternal, the most essential of all essences, higher than the highest, and beyond the range of mind, speech, and sight. (6.44)
O Goddess, it is eternal bliss, uninterrupted, incomparable, boundless, and supreme; it consists of Śiva and Śakti, being both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and possessing attributes (saguṇa).
The God who has the form of consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar, appears to yogis in the form of meditation as the shape of a lamp-flame. (6.46)
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Goddess, eternal and composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), with terrible fangs, a formidable mouth, a lolling tongue, and four arms. (6.47)
Her left upper and lower lotus-hands hold a freshly severed head and a sword, while her right upper and lower hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (6.48)
She has the luster of a dark blue cloud, is slender, possesses a terrifying voice, and is naked; she is smeared with dripping blood from a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck.
She who is terrifying with a pair of severed heads used as ear-ornaments,
and who is adorned with three eyes shaped like the orbs of the rising sun.
Her face was made radiant by streams of blood flowing from her two corners of the mouth;
she had disheveled hair, a smiling countenance, and dwelt in the cremation ground as her abode. (6.51)
She wears a girdle fashioned from the joined hands of corpses, her face is smiling, and she stands upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse. (6.52)
Afflicted by love, she sat down for the sake of pleasure with Mahākāla,
while she was surrounded on all four sides by jackals making terrible howls.
With a face exceedingly serene, her lotus-like countenance smiling,
she is right there as the Unstruck Sound (Anāhata), possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Above that, O slender one, is the peak, which is the supreme digit (kalā) in the form of the syllable *cih*.
One should contemplate oneself as united and become one with her. (6.55)
Proceeding by way of the path of Brahman (brahmamārga) through the sequence of piercing the *liṅgas*,
it possesses the brilliance of ten million suns and the coolness of ten million moons.
That nectar and its emission, characterized by supreme bliss, having gone to the divine Kulākula, should enter Kula once again. (6.57)
For one who practices thus with certainty day after day,
there appears within the lotus of the mūlādhāra a most beautiful triangle.

One should meditate on the Kuṇḍalī-śakti above that, possessing a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning, while [the soul] wanders at will within its midst, resembling ten million rising suns.
One should meditate upon that beautiful goddess of the gods within a triangle of nectar-streams, having the form of a sleeping serpent and endowed with three and a half coils.
Having repeatedly projected their power, which has its abode in the lotus-born [Brahmā], into this [universe] by means of themselves,
those whose hearts are fixed on it contemplate it in succession until the end of the cosmic dissolution,
culminating in eternal bliss.
One should meditate on the form of Consciousness situated within a sword, mallet, great lotus, and lotus, resembling a fresh rain-cloud and being the sole path to the way of liberation;
she who is directly Dakṣiṇāmūrti, seated upon a swan resting in a great lotus in the sky.
Having drunk the flood of divine nectar, one should enter once again the central region of the family.
In each wheel, in due order, one should satisfy those deities—Ḍākinī and all the others—in the lake of nectar with all the [offerings].
One should satisfy that Kuṇḍalinī who resides upon all the petals.
In the moon, above that, in the Vaidhṛti yoga, in the Nāda, and indeed in the Nādānta.
Furthermore, when the body is capable of perceiving the sphere of the jewel,
one should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
In that very supreme ether, which is nourished by the highest nectar,
he should reveal the true nature of the Self, even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like.
Thus should the practitioner of mantra, joined in yoga, reflect; of this there is no doubt.
Completely liberated from all sins, he beholds his desired goddess. (6.64)
Within six months, all accomplishments shall arise and one perceives the Self;
at the end of a year, the eighteen great siddhis will come to pass.
One should thus contemplate the Goddess, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self;
she is Śaṅkara himself in person, and she is the imperishable Viṣṇu. (6.66)
"He alone is the supreme Brahman; he alone is the highest deity.
Thus, O Goddess Maheśvarī, the Yonimudrā has been described to you.
Within a year one shall obtain perfection and attain the fruit of all fulfilled desires.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kubjikātantra.
The seventh chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Lord, Ancient One!
And I wish to hear about the state of being, especially regarding the deity.
"By what disposition, O Lord of Gods, does a deity become pleased?
I wish to hear all of that; let it be told, O Beloved of Life. (7.2)
Śiva said:
"Bhadra, Bhadra! I shall speak what is auspicious, O lady of pure smiles; out of affection for you, I shall speak, O beautiful one, so listen with attention. (7.3)
Having known this very thing, Viriñci undoubtedly becomes the creator of the universe;
Viṣṇu performs its preservation, and Rudra, moreover, is the destroyer. (7.4)
Having understood this, the most excellent of practitioners brings the world under his control;
he alone is worthy of veneration in this world, he alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 7/5 ||
And the state of being, O Goddess, is threefold according to the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu).
One should meditate upon the entire universe as having the form of the deity, O beautiful lady of the gods. (7.6)
One should perceive the entire world as the form of the female (strīrūpa) and the person (puruṣa) as the form of Śiva;
one should hold the goddess Pārvatī in the heart and the one in the form of Śiva upon the head. (7.7)
He who meditates upon non-duality is himself of the nature of the deity;
for him, there is constant bathing, constant giving, and the recitation and worship performed at the three junctions of the day.
O Goddess, one should wear pure clothing;
likewise, one should possess firm knowledge of the Vedas and the Śāstras, as well as [devotion] toward the Guru and the Deity. (7.9)
O lady of pure smiles, firm knowledge of the mantras, as well as the worship of the ancestors and the gods, the Vaiśvadeva offering, and the Śrāddha ceremony must be performed daily. (7.10)
O Goddess Maheśvarī, one should contemplate friend and foe as equal;
O Maheśānī, one should avoid [the consumption of] food from everyone. (7.11)
O Maheśānī, the food of the guru should be consumed for the sake of attaining all perfections;
O Mahādevī, one should avoid a miserly person and one who is cruel.
Upon seeing one who reviles the deities, one should not engage in conversation with them;
O Goddess, one should speak the truth and never anything false. (7.13)
One should worship the beautiful goddess solely with a divine disposition;
O Goddess, the wise man should contemplate the propitiation of the Guru every day. (7.14)

Everywhere, one should bow to the Guru, who is worthy of worship by the deities and whose nature is that of the Supreme Being; wherever he may reside in a single village, one should prostrate before the Guru at the three junctions of the day.
O Maheśānī, O fair-faced one, one should pay homage as if to a guru;
having seen the soles of the feet of women, one should always regard them as being like the guru. (7.16)
O Goddess, one should have the body of the supreme Gandharva deity fashioned, anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned, and exceedingly beautiful. (7.17)
One should avoid conversation with the wives of others and instead always honor the beautiful wife of the sun with the quality of goodness. (7.18)
O Maheśānī, O beloved of Hara, listen to the state of heroism;
O Great Goddess, there is no other deity within my body. (7.19)
He should be dressed in red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, and marked with the triple line (*tripuṇḍra*) made either with ashes or with red sandalwood paste. (7.20)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, adorned on all limbs with rudrākṣas, one should become Bhairava alone and worship the eternal Goddess. (7.21)
And one should offer oblations daily for the sake of attaining the state of divinity; having taken up the pledges (*samaya*), O Maheśvarī, at the beginning of worship and other rites. (7.22)
O Maheśvarī, worship should be performed at midnight;
likewise, O Maheśvarī, having beheld the Kula-tree, [worship] should be performed. (7.23)
O Maheśvarī, one should perform prostration and salutation every day;
one should worship the Goddess at night, and never during the day. (7.24)
O Maheśvarī, at night, with one's mouth full of betel, one should recite the mantra;
O Maheśānī, one should offer everything to the Supreme Goddess.
Those who delight in the state of beasts and are merely of animal form should never touch the ritual diagram (yantra) or the rosary (mālā) at night. (7.26)

There is always doubt regarding the offering of oblations and doubt regarding the Tantra; there is the notion that the mantra is merely a collection of letters, and constant lack of faith toward the Guru. (7.27)
O Goddess of gods, one should always maintain the perception of the stone in the image as the deity;
the worship of the deity is performed with a mind free from worldly desire. (7.28)
O Maheśvarī, one should always perform ritual bathing with ignorance, daily emaciation of the body, and the utterance of mantras that disparage all beings. (7.29)
That very same [nature] is proclaimed as the lowest when it is the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva);
the divine state (divyabhāva) is the highest, and the heroic state (vīrabhāva) is the intermediate. (7.30)
O Goddess, the state of being a bound soul (paśubhāva) is indeed the lowest; of this there is no doubt.
Mantras established in the state of the bound soul consist merely of the forms of phonemes.
And one should cultivate, O Maheśānī, the supreme state of being the deity;
having seen the Kula, O Maheśānī, especially the Kula-tree.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, one should pay homage to the family home and to a woman of the lineage who is an expert in the Tantras and Mantras, O Great Goddess. (7.33)
O fair-faced one, one should pay homage to a messenger devoted to the sacrifice, or likewise to a courtesan or an unchaste woman, whether she be old or young. (7.34)
By worshipping the maiden, one should always be endowed with devotion, beginning from five years of age until she reaches twelve. (7.35)
O Goddess, that maiden shall be the illuminator of her own true form, beginning from six years of age up until she is nine years old. (7.36)
And for that very purpose, O Great Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal of the practitioner, [this should be done] beginning from the eighth year until the thirteenth year. (7.37)
One should recognize her as a young woman and perform worship toward her;
she is one who has reached ten years of age and is up to sixteen years old. (7.38)
One should recognize that young woman as equal to a goddess and contemplate her as such; for he who gives food, clothing, and likewise water to a maiden [attains great merit]. (7.39)
O Goddess, one who gives food equal to Mount Meru and water as vast as the ocean,
as well as thousands of millions of garments, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Indeed, for one who gives articles of worship to a maiden, the deity, being satisfied, shows compassion toward him as if toward a son. (7.41)
O Goddess of the Gods, having seen an Aśoka tree, a Bilva tree, and Śivā, one should perform a prostration for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (7.42)
O Goddess of the gods, one should pay homage to Bhalluka, Śaṅyacilla, and Gṛdhra, as well as Mahākālī; thus one shall obtain victory in battle. (7.43)
One should especially pay homage to a crossroads and a cremation ground;
having gone there, O fair-faced one, one should pay homage to the Avadhūta.
Always seeing one who desires [to give], one should speak sweetly;
giving and receiving constitute merit, therefore one should practice giving to him. (7.45)
O Great Goddess, without the *samaya*, there can never be power;
therefore, one should receive it with great care—of this there is no doubt. (7.46)
Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all Āgamas;
O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me of the Siddhapīṭha.
Śaṅkara said:
Listen with careful attention, O devoted wife, to the Siddhapīṭha, by the mere practice of which one becomes the lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). 7.48.
Māyāvatī, Madhupurī, Kāśī, Gorakṣakāriṇī, Hiṅgulā as a great pīṭha, and likewise Jālandhara again. (7.49)
Jvālāmukhī is a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), and Nagarasambhava is a sacred seat;
likewise, O Dear One, Kāmagiri is a great sacred seat, as is Godāvarī. (7.50)
O beloved, [there are] Nepāla, Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahāvarṇa; Ayodhyā, Kurukṣetra, and the heart-stealing Siṃhanāda. (7.51)
Maṇipūra, Hṛṣīkeśa, Prayāga, Tapovana, Vadarī, Mahāpīṭha, Ambikā, and Urddhvamanaka. (7.52)
Triveṇī, Mahāpīṭha, Gaṅgāsāgarasaṅgama, Nārīkola, Virajā, and Uḍḍīyāna, O Maheśvarī. (7.53)
O fair-eyed one, one should know Kurugrāma as Vaidyanātha;
it is the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) of Kāmarūpa, which bestows the fruit of all desires. (7.54)
O Goddess, in the Kali age, this Kāmarūpa is remembered as yielding swift results;
having taken the garment of Kāmākhyā, one should perform recitation and worship. (7.55)
O Goddess, one shall obtain every desire fulfilled; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus has it been told in brief, O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion. (7.56)
Out of affection for you, I shall speak, O eternal one, within a state of devotion.
Pārvatī said:
Now I desire to hear; speak, O beloved of my life. (7.57)
"O God, protector of the worlds, [tell me] the rule regarding flowers.
Śaṅkara said:
"O Goddess, beloved of Hara, listen to the rule regarding flowers. (7.58)
O Goddess of the gods, Ambikā is certainly well-pleased by the offering of the aśoka, the lotus flower, the campaka, and the nāgakeśara. (7.59)
The *dhūstūra*, the *mālatī* flower, the *jātī*, and likewise the *yūthikā*;
the *vakula*, the *tagara*, the *madhu* flower, and the *vasantikā*. (7.60)
The kahlāra, karavīra, vandhūka, and lavaṅgaka flowers, as well as the japā flower, O Goddess of Gods—and especially red flowers—[are to be offered]. (7.61)
The greatness of Aparājitā cannot indeed be described;
O Maheśānī, the bilva leaf is composed of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (7.62)
Whatever fruit may arise from the gift of gold in the form of flowers, one certainly obtains that same fruit by offering a single bilva leaf. (7.63)
By the offering of a Java flower, one obtains the fruit of fine silk garments;
by the offering of a lotus flower, one is honored in the world of Gaurī. || 7/64 ||
The wise practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice with lotus flowers and javā flowers;
O Goddess of the Gods, he should offer red flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
One who always offers with devotion to the Goddess whatever beautiful flower there may be, whether born of water or born of land, shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha). (7.66)
And one should indeed give it, O Maheśānī, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Kubjikātantra.
The eighth chapter.
Pārvatī said:
O Mahādeva, Lord of the Universe, Master of Life, Supreme Lord!
For the benefit of practitioners, reveal this sādhana to me.
Śaṅkara said:
O Goddess, in the Kali age there are many kinds of spiritual practices that bestow full fruit;
however, one should perform the practice solely through the state of a hero (vīrabhāva). 8.2.
O Great Goddess, on a Saturday coinciding with the eighth day of the dark fortnight, at the dead of night at a most formidable crossroads, the wise man should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
O Sovereign of the Gods, [this is] the ten-syllable great mantra of Ugrā;
her worship is performed with black flowers or with flowers from a cremation ground.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform everything according to the Mahācīna method;
furthermore, one should offer oblations with blue flowers one hundred and eight times.
Therefore, one should cast that [substance] along with those mantras into the enemy's house;
within ten days, the destruction of the enemy will certainly occur. (8.6)
Having uttered the word *māyā*, the letter *kṣa* follows immediately after;
it is then encapsulated (*puṭita*), O Great Goddess, and consecrated a hundred times once more. (8.7)
Having performed the recitation, O Goddess, one should cast [the offering] and perform the animal sacrifice (paśuhoma);
O Maheśānī, on the day of the Kula-astrological period, one should use the Kula-substances, O Maheśvarī.
O Maheśānī, having placed five skulls at the root of a banyan tree and having prepared a seat there, one should perform the worship. (8.9)
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times, the wise practitioner should perform a fire sacrifice (homa),
O Goddess of the Gods, especially with black flowers and hibiscus flowers.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should perform the worship according to the very rapid sequence;
at midnight, the man should have his hair loose and wear a tiger skin.

The mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Śiva (Śrīṃ), the seed-syllable of Vighna (Hrīṃ), and Tārā (Oṃ) encased within it, consecrated one hundred times, should be placed upon a severed head and cast into the house of the enemy. (8.12)
O Goddess, within seven days it will certainly meet its destruction;
O Great Goddess, likewise on the eighth lunar day, on a Saturday, or at night.
O Supreme Goddess, one should fashion a figure of a man out of flour;
having prepared a seat there, one should perform the prescribed worship. (8.14)
O Supreme Goddess, having taken his seat at the root of an Aśvattha tree, the wise practitioner should mutter the mantra a thousand times and perform a hundredfold oblation with flour-cakes.
Having taken the remains of the *homa*, listen, O Supreme Goddess:
having wrapped the cloth with another cloth, one should bind it with a red thread.

O Maheśānī, one should cast [the bone] into the house of an enemy; it will certainly go to destruction. On the day of the week of one's own family-nakṣatra, O Great Goddess, even on an unprepared funeral pyre, [it should be cast]. 8.17
Having first performed the armor-rite (*kavaca*), one should perform worship there;
having recited [the mantra] six thousand times, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations. (8.18)
O Supreme Goddess, one should mutter the great mantra of Mahākāma;
having worshipped with black flowers, one should offer oblations with fresh ginger.
Furthermore, having taken that bone and empowered it seven times with mantras, one should cast it into the house of the enemy; this is the supreme method for their eradication.
Having taken wood from a cremation ground, one should prepare a seat there;
and upon that seat, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having prepared the site for the funeral pyre, one should perform worship there;
one should recite the mantra six thousand times and certainly perform the fire-oblation with the enemy's name. (8.22)
O Maheśānī, O Sureśvarī, according to the family tradition, one should perform the fire sacrifice with black flowers at midnight on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*), O lady of excellent limbs, one will certainly delude the enemy.
O Goddess of the gods, the wise practitioner should perform the *homa* with *kulapuṣpa*. (8.24)
A wise person should recite the eight-syllable mantra of Śmaśānakālikā one thousand and eight times; by this, he will certainly delude his enemy. (8.25)
O Maheśānī, on Saturday, having carefully taken hold of a skull, the wise one should recite the great eight-syllable mantra two thousand times. (8.26)
O Goddess, one shall certainly delude an enemy after three months;
having taken a cow's skull, one should then write the name-mantra.
O Goddess, by reciting [the mantra] eight thousand times, one will certainly destroy an enemy;
furthermore, one should offer oblations with blue flowers one hundred and eight times.
Alternatively, O lady of excellent complexion, listen to another way:
[the period] beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise. (8.29)
Having encased [the name] with those mantras, one shall crush the enemy in an instant, beginning at the time of twilight until sunrise. (8.30)
One should perform the recitation of the mantra in both forward and reverse order;
one should offer oblations with black flowers until the eradication [of the enemy] occurs. (8.31)
Within eight days, the destruction of enemies occurs for certain;
O beautiful goddess, one should perform the recitation after encasing [the mantra] with the Mātṛkās. 8.32.
The wise one should recite it by its name both forward and backward;
within ten days, the destruction of the enemy will certainly occur. (8.33)
O Maheśānī, on a Tuesday, having gone to the midst of a cremation ground,
one should worship the Yoginī there and then worship Bhairava.
Having worshipped Deveśī there, one should worship Tāriṇī there;
and having worshipped Kṣetrapāla, one should worship Tāriṇī there. (8.35)
O Goddess of the Gods, O Eternal One, one should perform the ritual of driving in the stakes (kīlaka) in the ten directions,
having uttered the twenty-syllable mantra with the name [of the deity] in the middle.
One should perform the recitation of the mantra five thousand times until the great night [of the new moon] arrives; one should continue the recitation for the destruction of enemies. (8.37)
One should offer oblations with red flowers; thus one crushes enemies in an instant.
O Goddess of the Gods, the wise one should worship the Lord of Gods while offering there. 8.38
O Maheśānī, on a Tuesday, having carefully taken a Śava (corpse) and having fixed a stake there with the root mantras, O Maheśvarī, [one should proceed].
There, one should meditate upon the Goddess, the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas;
having worshipped Bhairava there, one should perform the ritual bathing of the corpse.
There, one should perform worship to the four stakes (kīlakas):
Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, Yoginī, and likewise Bhairavī. (8.41)
O Great Goddess, a wise man should contemplate a corpse without a woman, and likewise a Brāhmaṇa or a Yavana without a Yavanī, O Goddess. (8.42)
And the corpse of an outcaste is the most excellent and praised for the act of battle;
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate Śiva there in the form of that corpse. (8.43)
O Goddess, O Mahādevī, grant success always, O All-pervading Lord!
Likewise, O Goddess, grant the perfection of mantra and protect me who has come to you for refuge. (8.44)
"O Mahādeva in the form of a corpse, obeisance to you, O Lord of all gods!
Having recited this, O Great Goddess, with a concentrated mind, one should mount the back of the corpse. (8.45)
There, one should perform recitation for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
having worshipped Karālī there, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

O Great Goddess, O Mistress of the Kula, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight during the month of Utkaṭa, whatever [rite] is performed, there shall be the accomplishment of all desires and goals. (8.47)
O Maheśvarī, having taken up a red garment and being naked, joined with the Śakti, one becomes the supreme Bhairava by means of the family substances (kuladravya). 8.48

Having first extracted the letter *kṣa*, endowed with the nasal resonance (*nāda*) and the bindu, [one should place it] in the south, O Goddess Ekālikā; after that follows the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*). (8.49)
O Goddess of gods, one should perform the worship especially with this mantra;
O fair-faced one, one should perform a recitation of a thousand repetitions of the Gajāntaka [mantra].
O woman of excellent complexion, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with red flowers;
there shall be the accomplishment of all desires and aims—he indeed is the supreme Bhairava. (8.51)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Kubjikātantra. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter. O Blessed One, Lord of the Masters of Life, expert in all tantras, creator of beings, please tell us the characteristics of one who has attained success in mantra.
Śiva said:
Listen, O blessed lady, I shall speak; let it be heard with full attention.
[I shall describe] the piercing of the knot of the heart and likewise the bristling of the hair.
In his name, he utters words with a faltering voice like one who is mad;
yet he possesses constant joy, constant faith, and is always adorned by the Vedas. (9.3)
And in a dream where one is joined with a deity through latent impressions (vāsanā), one perceives that very [deity];
subsequently, through the connection with ignorance, one perceives knowledge. (9.4)
The knowledge born from that attains stability and becomes firm once more; through the constant contemplation of the deity, the expression of compassion arises. (9.5)
Always beholding the deity for the sake of accomplishing the state of the deity, one possesses divine knowledge within the body and always performs the propitiation of the deity. (9.6)
He who perceives that which is undisturbed and equanimous is wise;
he perceives equal knowledge toward both a clod of earth and gold. (9.7)
He alone is the best of practitioners, liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, in the contemplation of the Formed, one should practice affection as if toward a son.
Having accepted as one's own that which is joined with hands, feet, and so forth, [one thinks]:
"In my body there is no other; the deity alone resides therein. (9.10)
There is no other god who ever stands upon his head at all times;
the Goddess, bearing the trident, protects him always. (9.11)
And thus, through the yoga of meditation or the yoga of knowledge, day by day, great wisdom arises within the heart of universal bliss. (9.12)
Practicing in this manner day after day, O Great Goddess, the practitioner should contemplate the formless through the formed. (9.13)
O Goddess, without the formed (sākāra), one does not perceive the formless (nirākāra); when the formed is present, everything has its root in the formed, and one perceives the formed. 9.14
O Goddess, through constant practice one attains the formless;
having attained the formless, one reaches the stainless state. (9.15)
O Goddess of gods, by means of the formless [state], the practitioner has accomplished his purpose;
thus, O Goddess, he is the one who can take any form at will through his entire being—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should become one who bears the banner of the deity;
by the mere meditation upon the deity, one attains the state of the deity. (9.17)
O Maheśānī, one should offer everything as an oblation to the Deity—whatever is established in the mind in the form of latent impressions and states of being. (9.18)
"And all that shall indeed come to pass, O Goddess; it is the truth, there is no doubt.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of my heart, Mahādeva, Supreme Lord, Ancient One! (9.19)
"O Lord of Gods, by what means will the perfection of mantra be certain? O Beloved of Life, please tell me the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā)."
Śaṅkara said: "Excellent, excellent! You have asked well; listen, O woman of excellent complexion.
O beautiful one, the accomplishment of my mantra occurs without effort."
I shall tell you all of that, truly, truly, and with absolute certainty:
O Maheśvarī, it is the seed-syllable of Ramā, the seed-syllable of the universe, and the seed-syllable of Vadhū.
The supreme practitioner should mutter the Puṭitaikajaṭā mantra;
O Maheśānī, the supreme practitioner should recite it eight thousand times. (9.23)
His speech shall consist of both prose and verse; of this there is no doubt.
Following that, there is the *kūrca* seed-syllable, the *śakti* seed-syllable, and thereafter the letter *kṣa*.
Having recited the mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti six thousand times in due order,
one shall indeed wander upon the surface of the earth having become a sovereign over all kingdoms.
One should inscribe the *dhūmā* mantra within the womb of a noble woman;
having made it recited by a capable person, the wise practitioner should chant it nine hundred thousand times.
He alone attains victory in battle; he is indeed the best of practitioners.
Furthermore, one should write the Dhūmā-mantra within the vulva of a woman of noble family (kulatrī). 9/27.
The wise one should recite it eight thousand times and then wander upon the earth;
he attains victory in battle and destroys his enemies in an instant. (9.28)
And one should write the mantra of excellent characteristics on the root of the forehead of a woman of noble family;
having seen that, the best of practitioners should again recite it five hundred thousand times.
Having encapsulated the supreme mantra of Dhanada with the Mātṛkās, he will undoubtedly become equal to a deity and a lord of men. 9.30
The wise one should recite it two thousand times; he shall become the lord of the entire kingdom.
Just as the gods move about, even so does the supreme practitioner. (9.31)
Then, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of a great lotus; furthermore, in the center of that eight-petaled lotus, one should write the mantra of Vagalā.
Having established [the mantra] in the heart, the best of practitioners should recite it;
thus he brings about agitation among the virtuous and crushes his enemies in an instant. (9.33)
The wise one should recite it eight thousand times, two thousand times, or nine thousand times;
he truly agitates the three worlds—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (9.34)
O Maheśvarī, having encased the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), the seed-syllable of Ramā, and the seed-syllable of the Guru with the seed-syllable of Dhanada,
the wise one should recite it a thousand times.
The great mantra of Surasundarī, which bestows full fruit in the Kali age, certainly brings about the paralysis of wind, the solidification of water, and the cooling of fire. (9.36)
Once the seed-syllable of Śakti has been purified, after three months, O Goddess, she who is beautiful in form will certainly come to him in the guise of a woman. 9/37.
O Goddess of gods, it bestows the full fruit without effort in the Kali age;
therefore, O Maheśvarī, it should be performed with every possible effort. (9.38)
O Goddess, the Great Queen Ratisundarī, endowed with the seed-syllable of Rati, should be recited eight thousand times; thereafter, one shall attain perfection.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action, so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). 9.40

And the five-limbed worship in the rite of *puraścaraṇa* consists of recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*), and the feeding of Brahmins. (9.41)
O Great Goddess, these five limbs bring happiness to practitioners;
through the great consecration, a person becomes capable in all rites. (9.42)
O Goddess, without the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka), one should not perform the contemplation of mantras;
therefore, with every effort, a person should become consecrated. 9/43.
O Great Goddess, during the autumn season, one should perform the contemplation of the mantra, beginning from the ninth day until the next ninth day arrives. (9.44)
The recitation of mantras (japa) should be performed for that duration; this is considered the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
It should begin on the fourth lunar day and continue until the ninth.
The recitation should be performed with pauses until the ninth day, beginning from the seventh. (9.46)
One should perform recitation and other rites for the sake of accomplishing all desires;
having begun at an auspicious time, one should carry out the practice of mantra-sādhana.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should perform the contemplation of the mantra;
with undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra from the moment of the first swallow until its release. (9.48)
Beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise, one should perform the recitation and carry out the practice of mantra-siddhi. (9.49)
Beginning from moonrise until the next moonrise occurs, one should perform the recitation and carry out the practice of mantra-sādhana. (9.50)
At night, with single-minded focus, one should recite the mantra while holding a betel-roll;
O Goddess of the Gods, during the day one should likewise recite it while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) throughout the entire night.
And this secret, O Great Goddess, bestows complete fruit in the Kali age;
having taken hold of the Śakti, O Queen of the Gods, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind. (9.52)
O Goddess, the secret has been told, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds; O Maheśvarī, it is the purification of Śakti by means of the Śakti-mantra.
Having first taken the vow, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the venerable *Kubjikā-tantra*, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord. || 0 || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter. Now begins the section on Obstacles. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Deity.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Now I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for a barren woman;
[the deities are] Raktamātṛ, Ṣaṣṭhī, Ḍāṅkura, and Jalakumāraka.
The Sage has declared that there are four types of obstacles for women;
I shall describe their nature according to the scriptures and in accordance with the prescribed rules.
People who desire progeny should perform the worship of these [obstacles] so that it may be fruitful.
The dismissal (or the worship of the exit), the re-establishment, and especially the offering of the bali-oblation.
Having understood the characteristics of the scripture, one should act according to the word of the guru;
otherwise, four kinds of obstacles arise from the time of menstruation.
Pain in the waist, as well as below the navel, in the flanks, and in the breast,
along with a discharge of blood and loss of potency due to *pradoṣa*, results in infertility.
If she remains without menstruation for one or even two months,
a deficiency of fruit arises due to the fault of merely having blood.
Thus ends the refutation of the mere redness [of the lotus]. || 1 ||
There will be a burning sensation in the eyes and hands, and especially in the genital region;
accompanied by saliva and blood, [the patient becomes] discolored due to the affliction of the *Ṣaṣṭhī* spirits.

Within one month she becomes fertile, and likewise after two months she may have her menstrual bath; otherwise, she will be impure with a blood-discharging womb, and there will be a corruption of the six [periods].
Thus ends the refutation of the genitive case [ending]. || 9 ||
There will be agitation, heaviness in the body, and frequent discharge of blood;
there will be pain below the navel, and the *bhāṅkura* [demon] will be the destroyer of one's sons.
If she becomes devoid of menses during the third or fourth month,
her limbs will become emaciated, there will be inflammation in her hands and feet, and defects such as sores and eruptions will appear.
Thus, [the existence] of the sprout is sublated. || 3 ||
Accompanied by pain and containing a fetus, with a withered body and little blood,
the state of being fruitless arises through the fault of Jalakumāra.
She is perpetually irritable, corpulent, and has menstrual periods that occur at irregular times; with heavy breasts and scanty menses, she suffers from the affliction caused by Jalakumāra.
Thus ends the section on the obstructors of the Jalakumāra. || 4 ||

Now, regarding the yantras for worship: having drawn these yantras— a triangle, a nine-cornered figure, a six-cornered figure, and a mandala-shaped one— one should invoke [the deity] preceded by the mantra.

Now, the meditation on Raktamātrī and Ṣaṣṭhikā: Oṃ, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the Mother of the World, who dwells in the maternity chamber— fair-limbed, with the moon as her crest-jewel, possessing three eyes, and with both arms placed upon her son.
Oṃ, I worship the Mistress of the Three Worlds, who is white in color, possesses two arms, resides in the lying-in chamber, drinks the menses of women, and is peaceful.
Now, the meditation on Ḍāṅkura and Jalakumāra:
Oṃ! White in color, with two arms, residing in the lying-in chamber, drinking the menses of women, peaceful—he shall be the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Now, regarding the ritual offerings: one should perform worship with the sixteen types of offerings for a period of three days,
using ornaments such as gold, silver, copper, and silk garments.
O Bhairavī, having thus performed the worship and other rites, the wise one should offer the oblation (bali) after reciting the mantra one hundred and eight or even a thousand times.
One should offer the threefold bali, as well as that which moves on land and in water;
one should diligently offer the bali and, being pure, consume the medicinal herbs.
(p. 15) Now, O lady of excellent complexion, listen as I shall proclaim the mantras and the method of their retention:
the syllable *tāra*, *māyā*, and likewise *lakṣmī*, followed by *ḍrūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the mantra.
The wise one should recite the mantra of Raktamātrī one hundred and eight times:
*Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (This is the mantra of Raktamātrī.
The mantra is considered to consist of the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), followed by the pair of *Kāma* (klīṃ), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and ending with *phaṭ svāhā*.
And this mantra of the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī bestows the attainment of a son.
Oṃ klīḥ klīḥ phaṭ svāhā. (Thus is the mantra of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
Oṃ hrīḥ, O Goddess, the seed-syllable of Vimalā, the mantra of Raktayoginī.
This great mantra of Ḍāṅkura should be recited ending with *svāhā*:
*Oṃ hrīḥ Vajrayoginī oṃ hrīḥ svāhā*. (Thus is the mantra of Ḍāṅkura. Then, [one should recite] *Tāraṃ* (*oṃ*), followed by *śūlāya vajra* for the trident, and then *hastāya* for the hand.
O Goddess, this mantra ending with "svāhā" is determined for the Water-Kumāra.
Oṃ śūlāya vajrahastāya svāhā. (This is the mantra of Jalakumāra. Now, regarding the medicine for afflictions: when [the time of] bathing has arrived, this supreme medicine should be administered.
And the root of red cotton, as well as nāgadāna.
A paste made from *viḍlavaṇa* and *mūla* combined with black pepper should be administered for three days, as long as the woman remains impure.
After bathing, one should apply the excellent *vārtākī* insect;
for twenty-one days, one should drink it mixed with milk.
For example—
one should drink two *tolakas* of honey, one *tolaka* of sugar, and one *tolaka* of ghee, all mixed together with milk.
The quantity of milk is proclaimed to be sixteen *tolas* in measure;
this applies equally to a woman whose children have died, one who has miscarried, and likewise one who is barren like a crow.
A woman who is childless, barren, or has been wronged by another shall take upon herself all the faults [of the offender], and eating the sacrificial post (methi) is the highest penance.
This medicine should be administered to a woman whose channels have been purified during a time other than her fertile period.
Aśvagandhā, vaṭavyāla, and the root of lakṣaṇa— or in its absence, vāṭyālaka and the white variety, O fair-complexioned lady—
one should eat these along with purātras, having ground them repeatedly in milk.
Her lineage will inevitably be devoid of men, and she herself shall bear children in her womb.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Kubjikātantra, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord.
