(Commentary) Now, the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
According to Yājñavalkya: With the hands between the knees, in a clean place, facing north or east.

A twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha. "With hands between the knees" means having placed both hands within the space between the two knees; Dakṣa describes that procedure as follows:
"Having washed his hands and feet, he should drink water three times after inspecting it, while keeping [the fingers] closed and [the thumb]..."

One should wipe the mouth twice with the root [part] of the hand; having first touched the mouth with three fingers, one should likewise touch the sense organs: the nose next with the thumb and forefinger, the eyes and ears repeatedly with the thumb and ring finger, and the navel with the little finger and thumb.
One should touch the heart with the palm, the region of the head with all [fingers], and the arms with the tips [of the fingers].

Regarding the performance of rites both in water and on land, Paiṭhīnasi states that the *ācamana* (sipping of water) should be performed while standing with one foot in water and the other on land. One who has sipped water while inside the water becomes pure only within; outside the water, he is not.

If one sips water only outside, one would be pure only externally; therefore, having performed one sipping inside and one outside, one should sip water for the feet, whereby one becomes purified in every respect. Then, according to the sequence prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, one should have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* and other auspicious formulas. Having thus honored the Brahmins with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—
With palms joined in reverence, he should say three times: "Oṃ, regarding this duty, the rite named so-and-so, may you declare it an auspicious day (puṇyāha)."

When the Brāhmaṇas have said, "Oṃ, auspicious day! Oṃ, auspicious day! Oṃ, auspicious day! the performer should worship the deities beginning with Gaṇapati. Then, [he should worship] the five deities beginning with Śiva.
One should worship the nine planets, beginning with Āditya, and the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra. Then,
having dispelled obstacles with the mantra "Oṃ Phaṭ," one should cleanse both hands with scented water and flowers, and perform three upward-sweeping claps of the hands.

*oṃ hrāḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīḥ śirase svāhā*; *śrīḥ śikhāyai phaṭ*. (Commentary)

"In this matter to be performed, namely, such-and-such a rite: Oṃ, may you grant your consent for prosperity. Thus three times. The Brāhmaṇas respond: "Oṃ, prosperity! Oṃ, prosperity! Oṃ, prosperity! may Tārkṣya with unharmed wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being."
Oṃ! We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, as the Lord of hosts;
we invoke you, the Lord of beloveds, as the Lord of beloveds; we invoke you, the Lord of treasures, as the Lord of treasures.
Vaso mama oṃ svasti oṃ svasti oṃ svasti.
Now follows the mantra for the recitation of the Rigvedic Svasti: Oṃ! May the Aśvins and Bhaga measure out well-being for us;
may the goddess Aditi, who is free from enemies, grant us well-being.
May Pūṣan, the Asura, grant us well-being; may Heaven and Earth, the mindful ones, grant us well-being;
we invoke Vāyu for our well-being.
May Soma, the lord of the world’s prosperity, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati, together with all his hosts, grant us well-being; may the Ādityas be for our well-being;
and may the Viśvedevas be for our well-being this day.
May Vaiśvānara, the Vasu Agni, be for our well-being;
may the gods and the seasons be for our well-being;
may Rudra protect us from distress with auspiciousness.
May there be well-being, O Mitra and Varuṇa; may there be well-being, O wealthy Pathyā Svasti. May Indra and Agni grant us well-being; may you bestow well-being upon Aditi.
May we follow the path of well-being like the sun and the moon.
May we be united with him who gives again, who slays, and who knows. May we ascend Tārkṣya— the bringer of well-being, whose wheel is uninjured, the great being, the crow of the gods,

I, with hands joined in supplication, take refuge in Saṅghomuca, Māṅgirasa, Gaya, Svastyātreya, and Tārkṣya in my mind. May there be well-being in our discourse; may we be free from fear. Om svasti, om svasti, om svasti.

*Oṃ, we take refuge in King Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni;

Then, thereupon, the three Vedas say:

The mind is the single light; it is the auspicious mantra of the kalpa.
Now follows the *saṅkalpa-sūkta* for the followers of the *Ṛgveda*:
"Om, may Sinīvālī, Rākā, Sarasvatī, Indrāṇī, and Varuṇānī— both of them— grant us well-being."

Now follows the *saṅkalpa-sūkta* of the Sāmavedins: "Oṃ! May the god Draviṇodas desire for you a full ladle; pour it out, or pour it down, or push it forward; from the beginning, the god has granted it to you. One should then begin the worship of the Śālagrāma and other [deities]. As for the water-jar (*ghaṭa*), however—
Having established the jar with the mantras for placing the jar, one should worship it.
Now, the installation of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*):

The practitioner, being pure, should prepare a jar made of clay, copper, or gold—neither too short nor too long, free from cracks, very firm, and clean. He should sprinkle it with the *Kāma-bīja* and likewise with the *Vāgbhava*.

One should purify it. Having placed the *kalaśa* according to one's ability, one should fill it with water by means of *māyā*. O Goddess of the Gods, one should place the preceptor there with this mantra: "Oṃ! All rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, lakes, clouds, streams, ponds, holy springs, and those flowing through heaven and the netherworld—all the sacred *tīrthas* [are present here]."

Let them place [the offerings] in proximity within the jar. One should present the sprouts with the *ramā* seed-syllable (*rām*) recited; the offering of fruit should be made with the *kūrca* mantra; stabilization is effected with the *strī* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*). One should offer vermilion with the fire-seed-syllable (*raṃ*) and the flower with the air-seed-syllable (*yaṃ*). Then, one should offer *dūrvā* grass with the root-mantra and perform the sprinkling with the *praṇavas*. [Hūṃ Phaṭ].

One should perform the striking with darbha grass using the mantra *svāhā*. For example: having sprinkled [the vessel] with *klīṃ*, one should purify it with *aiṃ*. Having established the water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon the mandala with *hrīṃ*, one should fill it with water with *hrīṃ*. One should perform the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrthāvāhana*) with the mantra *oṃ gaṅgādyāḥ*. Having offered a sprig with *śrīṃ*, [one should strike it] with *hūṃ*.

Having offered the fruit with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should place the water-pot (*kalaśa*). With the syllable *strīṃ* one performs the stabilization; with *ram* one offers vermilion (*sindūra*); with *yaṃ* one offers flowers. One should offer *dūrvā* grass with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) of the respective deity. With *oṃ*, one sprinkles [the vessel];
with *oṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should strike it with *darbha* grass.
Now, as for the general *arghya*:
having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square on one's left, [one offers] there with "Oṃ, to the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*)."

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ anantāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ kūrmmāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should wash a vessel made of copper or other materials with the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*.
Then, having placed the vessel together with its base upon the mandala, one should worship it with water using the mantra *namaḥ*, [offering] *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains, scents, and flowers.
Having prepared the *arghya* offering and established it with the *aṅkuśa* mudrā,
one should place *dūrvā* grass, rice, fragrance, flowers, and so forth upon it, and then display the *dhenu* mudrā over that water.
One should perform the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrtha-āvāhana*) with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. Having invoked the sacred water with the mantra beginning "Oṃ Gaṅge...

and so forth, one should then worship it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) once more, one should worship [the deity] in the southeast mandala, in the northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions. Then, having recited the root mantra seven times—
Having purified oneself with that water and sprinkled the ritual implements, one should begin the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*):
*oṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*; *oṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ*; *oṃ kṣīrasamudrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ kalpavṛkṣāya namaḥ*.
(Vyākhyā) Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva Godāvari Sarasvati | Narmade Sindho Kāveri, be present in this water!
Having thus invoked the holy waters from the solar disc, [one offers] sandalwood paste and flowers with the mantra "Oṃ."

Having poured [the water] into that vessel, one should display the *dhenumudrā* while uttering "Vaṃ," and then recite the *praṇava* "Oṃ" eight or ten times over it. Then, having sprinkled the door with that water while reciting the mantra "Phaṭ," one should worship it, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the deities of the door. Oṃ.
"Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa. With "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā," one should worship in the southwest (nairṛtyāṃ).

Then, by beholding with divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*) using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should dispel divine obstacles; with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," obstacles moving through the intermediate space (*antarīkṣaga*); and with three slaps of the left heel on the ground, terrestrial obstacles (*bhauma*).
Having recited "phaṭ" seven times, one should scatter parched rice, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains—
or simply take up only rice— and say: "Oṃ, may those spirits depart who dwell upon the earth."
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having recited this, one should scatter them; then, one should perform the purification of the seat.
Now, the purification of the seat (āsana-śuddhi):

"Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Lotus Seat of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti). Having thus worshipped the seat and taken one's place upon it, one should recite: "The seer of this seat-mantra is Merupṛṣṭha, the metre is Sūktapaṅkti, and the deity is the Tortoise (Kūrma)."

The application is for the formal occupation of the seat (*āsana-parigraha*). Having recited: "Oṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. You, in turn, support me eternally; make this seat pure," one should sit down in the *svastika* posture or another suitable manner. Then:
With palms joined in reverence:
on the left, *oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*, *oṃ paramagurubhyo namaḥ*, *oṃ parāparagurubhyo namaḥ*, *oṃ parameṣṭhigurubhyo namaḥ*; on the right, *oṃ gaṇeśāya namaḥ*; in the center—

Having recited the root mantra, one should offer salutation with: "Obeisance to [Name] Devatā. Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Śiva, and the other five deities; the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) beginning with Indra; the nine planets (navagrahas) beginning with Āditya;
the ten incarnations (daśāvatāras) beginning with Matsya; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; and Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Lakṣmī.
One should worship Sarasvatī as well. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Now follows the *bhūtaśuddhi*:
having purified both hands with sandalwood paste and flowers while reciting the mantra "Phaṭ," one should perform three upward claps of the hands.
Having made the offering and performed the binding of the ten directions with finger-snaps, [recite] the root mantra:
(p. 18) *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ | oṃ jvālāya oṃ namaḥ | adharmāya namaḥ | oṃ*.

Salutation to Ignorance (Ajñāna). Om, salutation to Dispassion (Vairāgya). Om, salutation to Sovereignty (Aiśvarya). Om, salutation to Non-dispassion (Avairāgya). Om, salutation to Non-sovereignty (Anaiśvarya). Om, salutation to Sattva (Saṃsattva). Om, ram, salutation to Rajas (Rajas). Om, tam, salutation to Tamas (Tamas). Om, salutation to the Intermediate Space (Antarāntana). Om, gam, salutation to the Self of Knowledge (Jñānātman).
One should worship with [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*. Then one should meditate again and invoke her: "Oṃ, O Blessed One, O Goddess Raktamātrī, come here, come here!
Having thus invoked her—(explanation).

Having contemplated oneself as a rampart of fire with the syllable *Raṃ* and a stream of water, and having placed both hands palm-upward on one's lap, one should [unite] the individual soul (*jīvātman*) residing in the heart— shaped like the flame of a lamp—
with the *Kuṇḍalinī* situated at the *mūlādhāra*, by way of the *suṣumnā* channel from the *mūlādhāra*.

Having pierced the six chakras— Mūlādhāra, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, Ājñā, and so forth— and having united [the vital breath] with the Supreme Self situated within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the head which faces downward,
one should [dissolve] therein the earth, water, fire, air, and ether, as well as smell, taste, form, touch, sound, and the nose...

Having contemplated that the twenty-four principles— consisting of the tongue, eyes, skin, ears, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), mind, intellect, and ego— as well as the [five] forms [of the elements], have dissolved [into the self], one should contemplate the seed-syllable *Yam*, which is the color of smoke, at the left nostril; then, by reciting it sixteen times, one should fill the body with air through that wind.
Holding the two nostrils, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) by reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times;

then, having completely dried up the body together with the black-colored personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) residing in the left side of the abdomen, one should exhale the air through the right nostril by reciting it thirty-two times. [The syllable] "raṃ" is for the right nostril.
Having meditated upon the fire-seed (raṃ) which is red in color, one should fill the body with air by reciting it sixteen times;
then, holding the nostrils, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) by reciting it sixty-four times,
and having burned the body along with the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) by means of the fire emitted from the *mūlādhāra*, [one should contemplate] that...

By reciting [the mantra] thirty-two times, one should exhale the breath through the left nostril along with the ashes. Having meditated on the lunar seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ*, white in color, at the left nostril, and having brought the moon to the forehead by reciting it sixteen times, one should hold the two nostrils and [meditate on] the Varuṇa seed-syllable *vaṃ*.

By reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times, one should form the entire body with the nectar flowing from that moon situated on the forehead, which consists of the letters of the Mātṛkā; then, by reciting the earth-seed syllable *laṃ* thirty-two times, one should contemplate the body as very firm and exhale the air through the right [nostril]. Thereafter—

Having established the individual soul (jīva) in its own place with the mantra "Haṃsa," one should contemplate oneself in the form of the Goddess, according to the count of the mātrās. As it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The Guru should unite [the soul] by means of the path of the Suṣumnā with the mantra 'So 'haṃ' into the Supreme Self, the abode of Śiva, which possesses a thousand streams."

Then, the wise practitioner should fill [the body] with the wind-seed syllable (ya), which is smoke-colored and marked with six dots, through the *iḍā* [nāḍī] for sixteen measures (*mātrā*). He should retain it in *kumbhaka* through the *suṣumnā* for sixty-four measures.
The mantra-master should exhale through the one called *piṅgalā* for thirty-two measures. And he should fill [again] by this same [method].

Having intentionally [visualized] the blue wind, one should [visualize] the red-colored seed-syllable of fire, which is triangular and marked with a svastika. By means of that practice of inhalation (*pūraka*) with sixteen measures, and by means of retention (*kumbhaka*) with sixty-four measures, one should burn the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*), which is situated in the left hip and has the luster of collyrium.
The head [of the corpse] consists of the murder of a Brahmin, and the two arms consist of the theft of gold.
(Root mantra) This is the silver seat: *oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ*, obeisance to the Goddess Raktamātṛkā. Thus.

Having worshipped with the sixteen offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight or one thousand times according to the sequence for the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra). Then, one should present the sacrificial offering (bali). One should give the threefold bali: that which moves in the sky, on the earth, and in the water.
After that, one should give the priestly fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Kubjikātantra, in the dialogue between the Goddess and Īśvara.
(The Explanation:
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor; the two hips are the violation of the Guru's bed;
the pair of feet is association with such persons; and the limbs and minor members are the various sins.
One should thus contemplate [the enemy] in the belly: his body covered with hair from minor sins (*upapātaka*), with red beard and eyes, cruel, and bearing a sword and shield;
one should then burn him away with the fire arising from the *mūlādhāra*.
Having thus thoroughly incinerated [the impurities] all around with thirty-two measures,
the practitioner of mantra should then exhale through the iḍā [left nostril], together with the ashes.
Within the left channel is the seed-syllable of the Moon, possessing a luster like that of the kunda flower and the moon.
Having joined [the breath] with the moon at the forehead (bhāla) for sixteen measures,
and then having meditated upon the seed-syllable of water (vaṃ) within the Suṣumṇā for sixty-four measures as a rain consisting of nectar in the form of the fifty letters;
Having thus contemplated the body with the mind by way of the piṅgalā path,

the practitioner of mantra should firmly lead [the breath] for thirty-two mātrās with the seed-syllable *laṃ*. Then, by means of the *haṃsa* mantra, he should lead it back again to its own place by that very same path.
Then, having brought the individual soul and the principles back, one should establish them in their respective places.
Now, the abbreviated *bhūtaśuddhi* is as follows; from the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Now, furthermore, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is prescribed by another method."

One should meditate upon [the lotus] blossomed by the syllable *praṇava* within the lotus of one's own heart— arisen from the stalks of the divisions of Dharma, beautifully adorned with the stalk of knowledge, endowed with the eight petals of the supernatural powers (*aiśvarya*), and possessing the pericarp of supreme dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Having placed that [light] situated in the pericarp, resembling the flame of a lamp,
one should meditate on the individual soul (jīvātman) in the heart; then, having contemplated Kuṇḍalinī at the base,
one should unite the self with the Supreme Self by way of the Suṣumnā path.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).

Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: For this Mātṛkā-mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), the consonants are the seeds (bījas), the vowels are the powers (śaktis), the unmanifest (avyakta) is the bolt (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is in the ritual placement of the letters (lipinyāsa).
On the head: Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the seer (ṛṣi).
At the mouth: Oṃ, salutation to the Gāyatrī metre.
In the heart: Oṃ, obeisance to the deity Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī.
In the secret place: Oṃ, homage to the seed-syllables of the veins (nāḍī).
At the two feet: Oṃ, salutation to the vowels and the Śaktis.
On all limbs: Oṃ, salutation to the unmanifested stake (avyakta-kīlaka).
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess of gods, hear [now] the Mātṛkā, which destroys all sins; one should perform its placement (nyāsa).
The seer of this Brāhma-mantra is said to be Gāyatrī."

The deity is the Goddess Mātṛkā; the seed-syllables (bījas) are the collection of consonants, while the vowels, O Goddess, are the powers (śaktis). One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). Then follows the ṣaḍaṅganyāsa.
Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the two thumbs.
iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā | (Mūla, p.
19) Chapter Twelve.
Now, regarding the procedure for the worship of Ṣaṣṭhī:
one should perform the *saṅkalpa* as before. One should draw the *yantra*. Then, one should worship the deities beginning with Gaṇapati.
Then, one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. Then, the *aṅga-nyāsa* [is performed] with: "Oṃ yāṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth.
Having performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should meditate:
"Oṃ! One should worship the Mistress of the Three Worlds, who is white in color, has two arms, resides in the lying-in chamber, drinks the menses of women, and is peaceful."
Having meditated thus and placed a flower upon one's own head, and having set out the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*).
Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti (the Foundation Power). Oṃ, salutation to Pṛthivī (the Earth). Oṃ, salutation to Kṣīrasamudra (the Ocean of Milk).
Oṃ, homage to the Kalpavṛkṣa (the wish-fulfilling tree). Oṃ, homage to Dharma. Oṃ, homage to Jñāna (knowledge).
Oṃ, homage to Vairāgya (dispassion). Oṃ, homage to Aiśvarya (sovereignty). Oṃ, homage to Adharma. (Commentary)
Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ Ūṃ, to the two middle fingers, Vaṣaṭ! Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ AIṃ, to the two ring fingers, Hūṃ! Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ AUṃ, to the two little fingers, Vauṣaṭ!
Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ, with both palms and backs of the hands, *astrāya phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other limbs.
"Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, homage to the heart," and so forth. Likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
"Aṃ and āṃ are in the middle of the *ka*-group; iṃ and īṃ are in the middle of the *ca*-group."
O Dear One, one should place the *ṭa*-group between *uṃ* and *ūṃ*, the *ta*-group between *e* and *aiṃ*,

and the *pa*-group— joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*)— between *oṃ* and *auṃ*. The *ya*- and *śa*-groups, together with their respective signs (*lakṣa*), should end with the *anusvāra* and *visarga*.
O Goddess, one should place the heart, the head, the crest, and likewise the armor; then one should apply the eye-mantra ending in "ṅ," followed by "namaḥ," "svāhā," and so on in sequence.
O Dear One, one should join [the mantras] ending in "vaṣaṭ," "hūṃ," "vauṣaṭ," and "phaṭ."
This six-limbed [practice] of the Mātṛkā is remembered as the remover of all sins.
Now follows the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (Antarmātṛkānyāsa):
One should place the sixteen vowels from *a* onwards, together with the bindu, upon the sixteen-petaled lotus at the root of the throat.
One should place the twelve consonants from *ka* onwards, together with the bindu, upon the twelve-petaled lotus at the heart.
One should place the ten syllables beginning with *ḍa*, together with the bindu, upon the ten-petalled lotus at the navel.
One should place the six syllables beginning with *va*, together with the bindu, upon the six-petalled lotus at the base of the genitals.
One should place the four syllables beginning with *va*, together with the bindu, upon the four-petalled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*.
One should place the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, together with the bindu, upon the two-petalled lotus between the eyebrows.
Likewise, it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should place the sixteen vowels upon the sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat."
One should place the twelve letters beginning with *ka* upon the twelve-petaled heart-lotus;
one should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* upon the ten-petaled lotus at the navel;
and one should place the six letters beginning with *va* within the six-petaled lotus situated at the *liṅga*.

One should place the four qualities to be described upon the base in the four petals: (Root mantra) Oṃ, salutation to ignorance; Oṃ, salutation to lack of dispassion; Oṃ, salutation to lack of sovereignty.
Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sattva. Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Rajas. Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to Tamas.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Inner Self (Antarātman). Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge (Jñānātman).
One should worship with the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namas*. Having again performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth, one should meditate.
Then, one should invoke her: "Oṃ, O Blessed Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, come, come here! Having thus invoked her, one should worship her with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).

The bathing mantra is as follows: *candra-hūḥ*, on the left side of the ocean of eyes, in the ninth hand, for the sake of the noble one, in the place of the vessel of impurity, the portion of victory in battle, let the poison or the vehicle carry away the bonds; [may there be] milk, the five peaks, and so forth, in the left.

"Fresh butter restores life; poison removes poison. By this [remedy], even insects and moths die. It causes delivery at the proper time and does not harm those who follow the prescribed procedure. Having recited this, one should bathe the woman whose child has died.
Then Śrī Bhairava, appearing like one dead yet possessing armor, said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures!"
O Lord, this is the rite of the goddess Dāmanī in her female form.
The Blessed One said:
May the goddess Dāmanī, who has assumed a female form and exists as the seed-syllable, protect [us] forever.
Hrīḥ Aiḥ Śrīḥ Vaiḥ Vaiḥ Vaiḥ Vaiḥ! Protect, protect [us] from all calamities caused by malevolent beings! Svāhā!
Hrīḥ! May Kālī protect all my limbs; obeisance to the King of Warriors, Svāhā!
Hrīḥ! May the Mother who possesses the form of an old woman protect me and remove [all obstacles] from every side.
This is the supreme secret, which grants the desires of the practitioner.
And it indeed brings about all forms of protection, especially from *bhūtas* and *pretas*.

A woman who is childless, or one who is as if dead, shall indeed come to have many sons with living offspring; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, as well as others who cause misfortune, [shall be subdued].
From afar they flee because of the wearing of this armor;
the very nature of living beings becomes like that of the dead, as if seized by death.
Therefore, it must be worn with great effort, for it destroys those who have lost their children.
"One who has given birth to a stillborn child should certainly wear this [amulet], having gone far away from that [child].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Armor for the Stillborn Child," in the Kubjikā Tantra.
